subject: anatomy
title: Biliary Tree Topography: Calot Triangle, Cystic Artery, and Bile Ducts

steps.tx: The extrahepatic biliary apparatus conducts bile from the liver into the duodenum. Right and left hepatic ducts emerge from the porta hepatis and unite to form the **common hepatic duct**, which is joined on its right side by the tortuous cystic duct from the gallbladder to form the common bile duct.
steps.say: The extrahepatic biliary apparatus transports bile into the duodenum. Right and left hepatic ducts join to form the common hepatic duct, which unites with the cystic duct to create the common bile duct.

vis.caption: Surgical anatomy of the gallbladder and cystic duct insertion into the biliary tree. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: The primary surgical triangle in biliary surgery is the hepatobiliary triangle of **Calot**. In its modern surgical definition, its boundaries are: superiorly the inferior visceral surface of the liver, medially the common hepatic duct, and laterally the cystic duct. Traversing this triangle is the cystic artery and the cystic lymph node of Lund.
steps.say: The hepatobiliary triangle of Calot is the primary landmark in gallbladder surgery. Bounded by the liver surface, common hepatic duct, and cystic duct, it contains the cystic artery and Lund lymph node.

rows: Inferior visceral surface of liver segment V
Mistaking CHD for cystic duct causes duct transection
Must achieve critical view of safety before clipping

steps.tx: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy mandates achieving the **critical view of safety** (Strasberg) before clipping or dividing any tubular structure. The hepatocystic triangle must be cleared of all fat and fibrous tissue, the lower third of the gallbladder dissected off the cystic plate, and exactly two structures (cystic duct and cystic artery) seen entering the gallbladder.
steps.say: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy requires achieving the critical view of safety before clipping. Dissecting the triangle to display only cystic duct and artery entering the gallbladder prevents bile duct transection.

vis.title: Three Criteria for Critical View of Safety

nodes.label: Clear Hepatocystic Triangle of All Fat and Areolar Tissue
Dissect Lowest 1/3 of Gallbladder Off the Liver Bed (Cystic Plate)
Confirm Exactly Two Structures (Duct and Artery) Enter Gallbladder
Safe Application of Clips and Division of Target Structures

steps.tx: The **cystic artery** is classically a solitary branch arising from the right hepatic artery within Calot triangle. However, anatomical variations occur in twenty-five percent of individuals: the right hepatic artery may course through Calot triangle as a tortuous Moynihan caterpillar loop, predisposing it to accidental ligation.
steps.say: The cystic artery usually arises from the right hepatic artery in Calot triangle. Variations occur in a quarter of patients, such as a tortuous caterpillar loop of the right hepatic artery.

left.title: Normal Cystic Artery (75%)
points: Arises from right hepatic artery in Calot triangle
Passes posterior to common hepatic duct
Divides into superficial and deep branches
Lies superior and medial to cystic duct

right.title: Moynihan Caterpillar Loop (15%)
points: Right hepatic artery loops downward into Calot triangle
Accidental ligation causes right liver lobe ischemia
Gives very short stubby cystic artery branch

steps.tx: The **common bile duct** (choledochus) measures approximately 7.5 centimetres (3 inches) in length with a normal lumen diameter of under six millimetres. It is divided into four anatomical segments: supraduodenal (in hepatoduodenal ligament), retroduodenal (behind first part), infraduodenal (in pancreatic groove), and intraduodenal (in duodenal wall).
steps.say: The common bile duct is roughly three inches long with a diameter under six millimeters. It consists of supraduodenal, retroduodenal, infraduodenal, and intraduodenal segments.

rows: In right free border of lesser omentum
Anterior to portal vein, right of hepatic artery
Standard site for open choledochotomy / exploration
Anterior to IVC; gastroduodenal artery to its left
Groove on posterior surface of pancreatic head
Compressed by carcinoma of the pancreatic head
Oblique course through medial duodenal wall
Impacted gallstones provoke biliary colic / jaundice

steps.tx: In the fourth (ascending) part of the duodenum, the duodenojejunal flexure is suspended from the posterior abdominal wall by a fibromuscular band termed the **ligament of Treitz** (suspensory muscle of the duodenum). Originating from the right crus of the diaphragm around the coeliac trunk, it marks the boundary between upper and lower gastrointestinal bleeding.
steps.say: The duodenojejunal junction is suspended by the ligament of Treitz, descending from the right crus of the diaphragm. It defines the anatomical border between upper and lower gastrointestinal bleeding.

left.title: Upper Gastrointestinal Bleed
points: Arises proximal to ligament of Treitz
Sources: peptic ulcers, varices, Mallory-Weiss tears

right.title: Lower Gastrointestinal Bleed
points: Arises distal to ligament of Treitz
Presents with hematochezia or maroon stool
Evaluated by colonoscopy or CT angiography

steps.tx: The third part of the duodenum crosses the midline between the abdominal aorta posteriorly and the superior mesenteric artery anteriorly. Narrowing of the aortomesenteric angle from severe weight loss or prolonged supine casting compresses the duodenum, precipitating **superior mesenteric artery syndrome** (Wilkie syndrome) with recurrent bilious vomiting.
steps.say: The third duodenum passes between the aorta and superior mesenteric artery. Acute weight loss narrows this aortomesenteric angle, producing superior mesenteric artery syndrome with bilious vomiting.

nodes.label: Severe Rapid Weight Loss Depletes Retroperitoneal Mesenteric Fat
Aortomesenteric Angle Narrows from Normal 45-60 to <20 Degrees
SMA Compresses Transverse Third Part of Duodenum Against Aorta
Postprandial Epigastric Pain, Duodenal Obstruction, Bilious Vomiting

steps.tx: Gallstones impacting in the gallbladder neck (Hartmann pouch) or cystic duct can cause chronic extrinsic compression and inflammatory erosion into the adjacent common hepatic duct, a rare syndrome known as **Mirizzi syndrome**. Patients present with recurrent acute cholecystitis complicated by obstructive jaundice and dilated intrahepatic ducts on cholangiography.
steps.say: Gallstones impacted in Hartmann pouch can compress or erode the adjacent common hepatic duct, causing Mirizzi syndrome. This produces cholecystitis with obstructive jaundice.
